title: Your Managers Say They're Coaching. Most of Your Reps Would Disagree.
summary: New data from Ambition's State of Sales Coaching in 2026 reveals that coaching frequency is a weaker predictor of quota attainment than a metric most organizations aren't watching nearly as closely: coaching coverage.
body_markdown:
Ask most sales leaders how their coaching is going and you'll get an answer about frequency. "Our managers do weekly 1:1s." "We have a monthly coaching cadence." "We coach bi-weekly."


It's a reasonable thing to track, and it is important… but it's not the most important thing.


New data from[Ambition's State of Sales Coaching in 2026](https://ambition.com/resources/the-state-of-sales-coaching-in-2026) — a survey of 312 sales managers, directors, VPs, and CROs — reveals that coaching *frequency* is a weaker predictor of quota attainment than a metric most organizations aren't watching nearly as closely: coaching *coverage* .


**The question isn't how often your managers coach. It's how many of your reps are actually getting coached.**


And the honest answer, for most organizations, is: fewer than you think.


### The Coverage Gap Nobody Talks About


When we asked revenue leaders what percentage of their sales reps receive at least one structured coaching session per week, the results were striking.


64% of organizations coach fewer than half their reps weekly. Nearly a third (31%) report that fewer than 1 in 4 reps receive weekly structured coaching.


Read that again: at most revenue organizations, the majority of salespeople are going weeks — sometimes months — without a meaningful coaching conversation.


It’s not because managers don’t care or don’t want to coach. Time is finite, the day is loud, and coaching naturally gravitates toward the reps who ask for it, the deals that are in trouble, or the top performers who are easiest to talk to. The quiet middle — the B-players who make up most of any sales team — tend to get missed.


The result is a coaching distribution problem that most organizations never measure and therefore never fix.


### Why Coverage Predicts Performance More Than Frequency


Here's where the data gets interesting.


When we looked at how coaching coverage correlated with quota attainment, the relationship was the clearest we found in the entire dataset:


- Organizations where 76–100% of reps receive weekly coaching: **54% report 71%+ quota attainment**
- Organizations where fewer than 25% of reps receive weekly coaching: **only 25% hit the same threshold**


That 2x gap between broad coaching coverage and narrow coaching coverage holds across the other variables we tested. It's more consistent than the coaching frequency finding and the AI adoption finding. Of everything we measured, getting coaching to more reps more consistently was the single strongest signal in the data.


The inverse is equally telling: when fewer than 25% of reps receive weekly coaching, more than half (53%) of those organizations fall into our lowest attainment bucket. Most of them *do* coach, but their coaching is concentrated on the wrong reps.


### The Squeaky Wheel Problem


Think about where a frontline manager's coaching time goes in a typical week.


The rep who's struggling on a deal gets pulled into a call review. The top performer gets a quick check-in about their pipeline. The newly promoted manager on the team takes up an hour working through a compensation dispute. By the time the 1:1 schedule rolls around, someone has a conflict, someone cancelled, and a third rep's session got pushed to next week.


This is normal. It's also how coaching becomes something that happens to some of your reps some of the time, rather than a reliable input across your whole team.


The organizations that have solved this problem have moved from relying on manager discretion to manage coaching coverage to building systems that make broad coverage the default. That includes automated 1:1 cadences, pre-scheduled coaching sessions that don't move, and visibility into which reps haven't been coached this week before the week is over.


Coverage isn't hard to achieve by accident — it requires a system.


### What to Do With This


If you're a revenue leader reading this, the most useful thing you can do today is ask a simple question: what percentage of my reps had a structured coaching conversation in the last 7 days?


If you don't have an easy answer to that question, you have a coverage problem — and your quota numbers are likely reflecting it, even if you can't yet see the connection.


The good news is that coaching coverage is one of the most fixable problems in sales management. You probably don't need new talent, new training, or a new compensation structure. You do need a system that ensures every manager touches every rep, every week, with enough consistency that "who got coached this week" stops being a guess.
